tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
# Display, canvas and runner gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- M5GFX reads a plain `uint32_t` colour as RGB888. `TFT_RED` and friends are
  RGB565 constants. The canvas holds pixels already byte-swapped into the
  display's order (`rgb565()` returns them that way), and the display runs
  with `setSwapBytes(false)`. A swap done by M5GFX on each push cost 10 ms of
  every frame (#23: pushes of 41-45 ms became 31 ms). `px_swap()` turns a
  canvas pixel into ordinary RGB565 and back: only code that reads colour bits
  needs it (the logo loader, `dump_main.c`, tests). A hue-sweeping palette
  stays a rainbow with its bytes swapped (red, green and blue rotate), so only
  pure black and white, or a colour you know (Maze's red flame, its green
  solving path), expose a wrong order on the device. Host frames cannot,
  since the swap happens in the push; compare them with `px_swap` applied.
- A hack that takes colour bits out of pixel values itself (Substrate's alpha
  blend, in `point2rgb`) breaks on swapped pixels without a compile error and
  without a crash. `substrate_single.c` swaps at `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground` so the hack sees ordinary RGB565; its golden-frame test
  fails if either is missing. Searching for `XGetPixel` finds none of this:
  dump every hack before and after a pixel-format change and `cmp` the frames.
  Pyro differs by a few hundred pixels, because it sorts projectiles by pixel
  value and so draws overlaps in another order.
- The display only gets the rows a hack drew. Every canvas write must go
  through `canvas_clear`, `canvas_point`, `hspan` or `canvas_paste_rect`
  (which record a span per row), or call `canvas_mark_dirty`, or the screen
  keeps the old pixels. The overlay text in `main.cpp` is the one deliberate
  bypass: it is written straight into `px`, marked by hand, and restored with
  `canvas_paste_rect`, which marks it again so the next push erases it.
  `test_push_present` replays every hack into a shadow display to catch a
  missed mark. M5GFX keeps a framebuffer for this panel and `endWrite` flushes
  one bounding box around everything written in a `startWrite` batch, so rows
  far apart must not share a batch (two corner pixels cost 11.7 ms together,
  0.1 ms apart). `push_plan` groups rows with a cost model fitted to device
  probes; its calibration shapes must include scattered rows, since compact
  rectangles cannot tell the models apart. Hacks that redraw unchanged pixels
  (CloudLife, Pedal) dirty nearly every row and gain little.
- The panel is round, so only the canvas's disc is pushed (issue #77).
  `canvas_set_disc` (in `main.cpp`) records each row's visible span: centre
  (w/2, h/2), and a pixel counts if any part of it is inside the circle.
  `push_plan` clips every dirty span to it and drops rows left empty. A hack
  with `sync_to_refresh` (Unknown Pleasures) still pushes whole rows, because
  its TE offset was swept for that push (#68). `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` turns off the
  push clip only, for an A/B: GL hacks still clear and fill only the disc
  (`gl.md`). Call `canvas_set_disc` before any `glshim_open`, which keeps a
  pointer to the spans. On the board: CloudLife's full frame 28.0 to 24.8 ms
  (26.2 to 28.4 fps), HexTrail 30.6 to 27.3 ms, Pyro 1.60 to 1.43 ms.
- Do not split a push into more batches than `push_plan`'s greedy grouping
  makes. Each extra flush in one push cost about 0.85 ms on the board, not the
  model's 17 us: a full disc frame in 19 bands took 39.9 ms against 24.7 ms in
  the greedy grouping's three, and per-row `pushImage` calls in one batch cost
  no more than one whole-image call (28.0 against 27.8 ms). The last flush of a
  push seems to finish while the hack draws its next frame; earlier ones are
  waited for. The cost model was fitted to single-flush pushes and cannot see
  this, so a split it rates cheaper can be slower.
- Hacks run on the Arduino `loopTask`, now set to a 16 KB stack in `main.cpp`.
  A hack with big local arrays can still overflow it (Rorschach's 9.6 KB did
  at 8 KB): the device reboots on that hack's first frame, and host tests
  cannot see it. Check the serial log for "Stack canary".
- `M5.update()` samples the buttons only when it runs and keeps no edge, so a
  press during a long hack step vanishes. `main.cpp` runs a 5 ms polling task
  on core 0 into `button_latch`, which needs the pin to hold a level for 30 ms.
  Reading the pin level inside a GPIO interrupt did not work: the release
  bounced and was counted as a second press. Check `press_waited` in the log.
- The runner caps a hack's delay at 10 s, and the loop credits only the push
  (31 ms; it was 41-45 ms between the byte-order fix and #23) against it,
  because a hack's delay is its pause after drawing. Compare device numbers
  with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: Pyro fell from 30 to
  23 fps with no change to Pyro.
- `runner_start` paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before
  `init`, as `screenhack.c` paints the window, or black if it has none.
  Substrate is white; every other hack asks for black or nothing.
- Overlay modes cycle on a tap: nothing, name badge, QR code, fps, battery. The
  badge, the QR code and the info line share the stamp/unstamp path, and
  `kPatchMaxH` (140) must cover the text block plus its outline: the badge
  is two lines, and `stampText` drops any line that would not fit. The
  battery is polled every 30 s (`M5.Power.getBatteryLevel()`; negative means a
  failed read, so the last good level stays). The QR code is encoded once at
  boot with M5GFX's `lgfx_qrcode` (`buildQr`, lowest version that holds
  `QR_URL`) into a 328 px white square, the biggest square inside the round
  screen. Each frame only copies it over the canvas and back (it reuses
  `infoPatch`, so that buffer is sized for the QR), and 328 rows are pushed
  every frame while it shows. The badge stamps 48 outline copies per frame and
  adds about 16 to 20 ms to `push=`. Read `wait=` as well as fps: a hack with
  delay slack (Galaxy) hides it, one running flat out (Squiral) does not.
- `lgfx_qrcode.h` (M5GFX's QR encoder, included at the top of `main.cpp`)
  defines `MODE_*`, `ECC_*` and `LOCK_VERSION`, which clash with other code, so
  `main.cpp` `#undef`s them straight after the include. Its init returns
  nonzero when the text is too long for a version; `buildQr` tries versions 1
  to 40 and, if none fits, leaves `qrPixels` null so the tap cycle skips QR.
- Overlay text (`main.cpp`) is stamped into the canvas, pushed, then the
  pixels under it are restored. Drawing on the display after `pushImage`
  flickered badly, because the next push erases it. The canvas must end each
  frame exactly as the hack left it.
- Tearing. The panel scans its memory 60 times a second and `pushImage` is not
  synchronised with it, so for a refresh the top of the screen shows one
  picture and the rest another. A thin line that moves a few pixels a frame can
  fall in the gap and vanish for a frame (Unknown Pleasures' flicker: a flat
  stretch of one line gone for about 17 ms). The panel's TE line is on GPIO 38
  (`OLED_TE`), M5GFX programs it (`0x35`, `0x44` at line 466) and nothing waits
  for it. It pulses every 16.82 ms for 1.1 ms. A full push is 20.6 ms copying
  into M5GFX's framebuffer plus 11.7 ms flushing to the panel (split by an
  outer `startWrite()` around the `pushImage`; the flush happens at the
  `endWrite`). `HackEntry::sync_to_refresh` (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`) starts
  the push `kTeSyncOffsetUs` after TE rises (`runner/te_sync.h`). Only
  Unknown Pleasures asks, because it costs up to a refresh of latency a frame.
- The offset (7.4 ms) is the middle of the clean window, found by a sweep:

# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic as copied held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and
  ran at 1.2 fps (it is registered again after issue #37, see `hacks.md`). A
  failed port that has its source and a measured row (Hypnowheel, Boing)
  still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed standalone. Measure on the
  device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- A `failed_ports.txt` name is the scorer's: the source file's stem
  (`companion` for Companion Cube), as the assessment's rows spell it. Check
  the cross appears after regenerating.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.
- `score_hacks.py` counts a hack as ported if `&<name>_hack` appears anywhere
  in the text of `g_hacks[]`, `#ifdef` or not, and then refuses one that
  `failed_ports.txt` also lists. A probe-only entry (Hypnowheel's
  `HYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`) goes through a macro defined above the array.
- `speed_backtest.py` stops with "hypnowheel: does not compile ... 'rotator.h'
  file not found": a dropped GL port counts in the backtest and is probed
  standalone, without the GL helpers' include path. `docs/speed-backtest.md`
  was last regenerated before Hypnowheel was ported, and was not regenerated
  for the CWaves batch either. The scorer also lists calls inside code that is
  never compiled (`XCreateBitmapFromData` in Cynosure's `DO_STIPPLE` block) as
  gaps.
- `score_hacks.py` skips the names in `OWN_HACKS` (our own hacks with no
  xscreensaver source, now `ad_flyingtoasters`) and still reports any other
  registry name it cannot scan as a typo. `speed_backtest.py` runs on the host
  only the registered hacks that have a device-measured row, so a `dump` build

SKILL.md

---
name: device-run
description: Use when flashing the StopWatch, pinning a hack or setting build flags (START_HACK, ROTATE_SECONDS, BADGE_NAME, QR_URL, toaster flags, GL_PROFILE), capturing the serial log, A/B testing builds with ab_flash.py, or reading fps, push, heap and psram on the device.
---

# Flashing and measuring on the device

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `pio run -e stopwatch`: build for the device. Add `-t upload` to flash.
  The device starts on a random hack; to pin one while examining it, prefix
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS='-DSTART_HACK=\"galaxy\"'` (a name from `g_hacks[]`,
  any case; an unknown name falls back to random and logs it). Rebuild without
  it afterwards, since the define sticks to the build. Unescaped quotes fail
  with "error: 'truchet' was not declared in this scope".
  It rotates to the next hack every 90 s (a button press restarts the count);
  `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5` shortens that for leak testing and `=0` turns it off. A
  pinned build still rotates, so add `=0` to measure one hack.
  The log prints `rotate -> <hack> heap= psram=` at each change. Combine flags
  in one `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` string.
  `-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod\ B.\"` sets the name badge text (default "Rod" over
  "Begbie"; `\n` starts a new line). Check a
  flag reached the binary with
  `strings -a -n 3 .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c '^Rod B\.$'`:
  plain `strings` skips anything under 4 characters.
  `-DQR_URL=\"https://example.com\"` sets the QR overlay's target (default the
  LinkedIn profile). Check it reached the binary with
  `strings -a .pio/build/stopwatch/firmware.elf | grep -c 'example.com'`.
  In a worktree session the harness refuses backslash-escaped flag values and
  `$(cat file)`. Use `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="'-DBADGE_NAME=\"Rod B.\"'
  '-DSTART_HACK=\"gears\"' -DROTATE_SECONDS=0"` with `.venv/bin/pio run -d
  firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` from the worktree root.
- Serial log: read `/dev/cu.usbmodem112401` at 115200 for N seconds into a file
  (a pyserial script run with `.venv/bin/python -I`). Run it in the background
  with absolute paths, since background shells ignore `cd`. Lines to read:
  `run <hack> fps= step= push= sync= wait= rows=` (ms per frame in the hack,
  the push, the wait for the panel's TE edge before a synced push (only
  Unknown Pleasures; not counted in `push=`) and the wait; mean canvas rows
  sent per frame, 466 being a full push,
  though overlay redraws made while waiting can push it higher)
  and `switch -> <hack> press_waited=`. An empty capture, or "Device not
  configured", means the USB port went away and came back (a flash, a crash):
  reopen it in a loop. Opening the port resets the board
  (`rst:0x15 USB_UART_CHIP_RESET`, even with DTR/RTS held low): the overlay
  returns to nothing and a random hack starts. To measure one hack, flash a
  pinned build (`START_HACK` plus `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), start the capture, then
  tap during it: the early windows are the baseline, the later ones have the
  overlay.
  Set `dtr` and `rts` to False on an unopened `serial.Serial()` before
  `open()`: a reopen loop without that once parked the chip in its bootloader
  (`boot:0x3 ... waiting for download`, screen frozen). Recover, or reset just
  before a capture to log from boot (a hack's `fprintf(stderr)` reaches the
  log), with `.venv/bin/python .platformio/packages/tool-esptoolpy/esptool.py
  --chip esp32s3 --port /dev/cu.usbmodem112401 --after hard_reset read_mac`.
- Flash with `pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > file 2>&1`, never piped through
  `head`, and check for "Hash of data verified". The button steps backwards
  (Pyro, then Lightning, then Drift...). Work out how long a restart takes
  from the hack's cycle count times its frame time (Substrate: 10,000 cycles
  at about 160 ms is 27 minutes) and capture that long, with rotation off.
- `ad-flyingtoasters` force flags (add to `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS`):
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_ART=0|1` (0 is 1-bit, 1 is colour) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_DONENESS=0|1|2` (light, medium, dark) and
  `-DAD_TOASTERS_SCALE=1|2` (2 is the default, with 6 flyers; 1 is the
  original size, with 10); a number outside those is an `#error`. It logs
  `ad-flyingtoasters: <art>, doneness=<level>` to stderr at start.
- To see where a GL hack's frame goes, add `-DGL_PROFILE`: a `glprof` line
  follows each `run` line with time per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill). Time left
  over is the hack's own code. To compare builds, `.venv/bin/python -I
  tools/ab_flash.py --hack Gears --seconds 60 --rounds 2 --out <dir>
  "a=-DGL_PROFILE" "b=-DGL_PROFILE -DFOO"` builds each variant pinned, flashes
  them in turn and tabulates the windows. It flashes: run it only with Rod's
  go-ahead. It builds each hack's variants from the working tree when that
  hack's turn starts, so leave `src/` and `tools/tinygl_patch.py` alone until
  the last hack has built. It compares flag variants of one tree: to A/B a
  change, put it behind a temporary `-D` switch (as `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` does).
  It takes one `--hack` per run: loop several from a scratchpad script run
  with `run_in_background`, and `touch` a done file at the end.
- `esptool` reads of the 16 MB flash need `--baud 921600` (about 3.5 minutes)
  and show no progress when piped.
- Another session may be using the board. Before flashing, run `lsof
  /dev/cu.usbmodem112401`: a "multiple access on port" upload error was
  another session's serial capture, and esptool's connect resets the board
  under it. Ask Rod before flashing over someone else's run.
- PlatformIO cleans the build directory, image and all, when
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` changes: an `-t nobuild -t upload` with other flags
  finds no `firmware.bin`. To keep several images, give each its own
  `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_DIR` (the build scripts all use `$BUILD_DIR`).
- Read `push=` from a hack's second 5 s window on: the name overlay is stamped
  inside the push timing while it shows, so the first window reads high.
- `heap=` and `psram=` are the reading at the end of a window, not a minimum:
  a hack with a long pause and nothing held in it (Celtic's 5 s `*delay2`)
  reads idle in every window. Sample while it works, or read `rotate ->`.
- Report a hack's lowest `fps=` window as well as its mean. HexTrail's step
  grows over a 65 s cycle: mean 15.3, worst window 10.8, and Rod saw an earlier
  build sag under 10 fps before the rotation moved on. Capture a full cycle and
  say which build the board holds when you stop.
- A boot is deterministic (same hack, layout and windows), so to compare two
  builds flash them alternately and compare window by window; one reading in
  three captures was an unexplained outlier, so never trust a single pair.
- Leak-testing with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=5`: internal heap falls about 26 KB
  during the first lap and then stays flat. Compare lap 2 with lap 3, not
  with lap 1. PSRAM should match exactly on every visit.
- To prove a device-only path the host cannot run (the ROM's `tinfl`), add a
  temporary `#ifdef` block after `printStats("boot")` in `main.cpp` that logs
  a checksum, compare it with one computed in Python, then `git checkout
  firmware/src/main.cpp` before pushing.

"""Flash builds of the firmware in turn and compare their serial logs.

    .venv/bin/python -I tools/ab_flash.py --hack CubicGrid --seconds 60 \\
        --rounds 2 --out /tmp/ab base= iram=-DGL_IRAM "prof=-DGL_PROFILE -DGL_IRAM"

Each `name=flags` is a variant. Every variant is built once, pinned to the
hack with rotation off (`START_HACK`, `ROTATE_SECONDS=0`), and its image kept.
Then, round by round, each image is flashed and the serial log captured for
`--seconds`. A boot is deterministic, so alternating builds and comparing
window by window is how this repo measures a change (AGENTS.md).

This flashes the device: run it only with Rod's go-ahead. It never touches
the partition table or `ffat`; `pio run -t upload` writes what a normal
upload writes.
"""

"""Makes BinaryRing's random scale a float literal.

`frand1()` is `random() << 1` times 4.65661287524579692411E-10, an exponent
literal, which tools/float_literals.py leaves as a double. Every particle calls
it twice a frame, so in the single-precision build each call would still be a
software double multiply on the board. The copied binaryring.c stays
byte-identical; firmware/patch_float_literals.py runs this on its text.
"""

OLD = "4.65661287524579692411E-10)"
NEW = "4.65661287524579692411E-10f)"


def float_random_scale(source: str) -> str:
    found = source.count(OLD)
    if found != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"expected 1 of `{OLD}` in binaryring.c, found {found}; has upstream changed?"
        )
    return source.replace(OLD, NEW)
/* Builds the unmodified binaryring.c, told the display is 24 bits deep, in
 * single precision (the ESP32-S3's FPU is single-precision only, so `double`
 * maths runs in software) and with its decimal literals made floats at build
 * time (tools/float_literals.py, and tools/binaryring_patch.py for the
 * exponent literal in frand1).
 *
 * The hack blends each anti-aliased hit into its own buffer of pixel values
 * at an alpha of 0.15 times the coverage. In its 16-bit path a hit adds less
 * than one 5-bit step of red or blue, which is dropped, so only green ever
 * builds up and the picture stays a dim green. In its 24-bit path (0xRRGGBB,
 * as on most X displays) the hits accumulate, so the wrapper gives it that
 * depth.
 *
 * Each pixel it writes to its XImage goes straight to the window instead,
 * packed to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565, and the frame's XPutImage into a
 * pixmap and XCopyArea to the window are skipped: the window then holds what
 * the copy would have put there. Those two full-frame copies took 130 of a
 * 240 ms step on the board (the XImage is 32 bits a pixel, which XPutImage
 * copies a pixel at a time), and they marked every row for the push. */

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

#include "screenhack.h"

#include "core/canvas.h"
#include "x11shim/pixmap.h"

static Canvas *binaryring_window;

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))

import xspirograph_patch as xp
import xs_vendor

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
UPSTREAM = xs_vendor.upstream(ROOT) / "hacks" / "xspirograph.c"

SAMPLE = """\
static Bool
go (struct state *st, int radius1, int radius2, int d)
{
  return cos(1.0);
}

#define min(a,b) ((a)<(b)?(a):(b))
"""


def test_go_is_replaced_and_the_rest_kept():
    out = xp.reduce_the_angles(SAMPLE)
    assert "% 360" in out
    assert "return cos(1.0);" not in out
    assert "#define min(a,b)" in out


def test_both_angles_are_reduced_before_the_multiply():
    out = xp.reduce_the_angles(SAMPLE)
    assert "spin = st->theta % 360;" in out
    assert "roll = (((radius1 * st->theta) - delta) / radius2) % 360;" in out


def test_it_refuses_a_source_without_go():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="upstream"):
        xp.reduce_the_angles("int x;\n")


def test_it_refuses_go_twice():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="upstream"):
        xp.reduce_the_angles(SAMPLE + SAMPLE)


@pytest.mark.skipif(not UPSTREAM.exists(), reason=f"needs {xs_vendor.UPSTREAM}")
def test_upstream_has_go_once_and_keeps_its_neighbours():
    text = UPSTREAM.read_text()
    out = xp.reduce_the_angles(text)
    assert out.count("roll = ") == 1
    assert "static void\npick_new" in out
    assert "#define min(a,b)" in out

content.content:
"""Lists the software-double calls in the device build's objects, by function.

The ESP32-S3's FPU is single-precision only, so `double` arithmetic and libm
calls become library calls (`__muldf3`, `sqrt`, ...) that cost tens to hundreds
of cycles. A wrapper that still shows them in a per-frame function has a
literal or a macro the single-precision header could not reach (`frand`,
`MAXRAND`, `M_PI`). This reads what the compiler produced, so it needs a device
build: `pio run -e stopwatch` from `firmware/`.

    uv run tools/softdouble_report.py              # every hack object
    uv run tools/softdouble_report.py galaxy_single x11shim/stroke
"""

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
OBJDUMP = next(
    (ROOT / ".platformio/packages/toolchain-xtensa-esp32s3/bin").glob(
        "xtensa-esp32s3-elf-objdump"
    ),
    None,
)
BUILD = ROOT / "firmware/.pio/build/stopwatch/src"

SOFT = re.compile(
    r"R_XTENSA_\w+\s+(__\w*df\w*|sqrt|floor|ceil|sin|cos|pow|atan2?|log|exp)\s*$"
)
FUNCTION = re.compile(r"^[0-9a-f]+ <(.+)>:")


def soft_calls(obj: Path) -> dict[str, Counter]:
    """Soft-double references per function in one object file."""
    assert OBJDUMP is not None, "toolchain not found: link .platformio into the repo"
    listing = subprocess.run(
        [str(OBJDUMP), "-dr", "--no-show-raw-insn", str(obj)],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        check=True,
    ).stdout
    found: dict[str, Counter] = defaultdict(Counter)
    function = None
    for line in listing.splitlines():
        if m := FUNCTION.match(line):
            function = m.group(1)
        elif (
            function
            and not function.startswith(".literal")
            and (m := SOFT.search(line))
        ):
            found[function][m.group(1)] += 1
    return found


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    if not BUILD.is_dir():
        raise SystemExit(f"no device build at {BUILD}: run pio run -e stopwatch")

"""capture.py <seconds> <out>: log the serial port, reopening if it drops."""
import sys
import time

import serial

secs, out = int(sys.argv[1]), sys.argv[2]
end = time.time() + secs
with open(out, "w", buffering=1) as f:
    while time.time() < end:
        s = serial.Serial()
        s.port = "/dev/cu.usbmodem112401"
        s.baudrate = 115200
        s.timeout = 1
        s.dtr = False
        s.rts = False
        try:
            s.open()
            while time.time() < end:
                line = s.readline()
                if line:
                    f.write(line.decode("utf-8", "replace"))
        except (serial.SerialException, OSError):
            time.sleep(1)
        finally:
            s.close()

 - `single_precision.h` renames the keyword `double`, not literals: `0.5 * x`
   is still software double. Braid's wrapper includes a copy of the hack with
   every decimal literal suffixed `f`, written at build time by
   `firmware/patch_float_literals.py` (`tools/float_literals.py`). Check a
   wrapper's object for `__muldf3` and friends with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm`.
-  The older wrappers (Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame, Substrate) have not been
-  checked.
+  `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` does that for every object in
+  the device build, by function: a count in a per-frame function is a literal
+  or a macro the header could not reach. It lists none in Galaxy, Discrete,
+  Drift, Flame, Substrate or Interaggregate now.
+- Three things hide soft double from `single_precision.h`, each found by that
+  report. `frand` (`single_frand.h`) and `MAXRAND`, `M_PI`, `M_PI_2` and
+  `M_PI_4` (`single_constants.h`) are macros with a decimal literal in their
+  body, past the literal pass; both headers are opt-in, since each moves the
+  wrapper's frames and pins. Exponent literals (`1e-6`, `1.0E5`) were skipped
+  by `float_literals.py` until Drift and Flame showed one each. And a struct
+  declared with `double` fields before the rename keeps them, so a float
+  `corners[j].x * size` plus a `double` `pos.x` is a software add: HexTrail's
+  `XYZ` (from `normals.h`) was 94 calls in `draw_hextrail`. Give the hack its
+  own float struct under the same name, and `normals.h` another name for the
+  double one (`hextrail_single_gl.c`; frames byte-identical). To find the line
+  of a stray promotion, add `-Wdouble-promotion -fsyntax-only` to a file's
+  compile command in `firmware/compile_commands.json` (`pio run -e stopwatch
+  -t compiledb`; delete the file afterwards, it upsets the editor).
+- `canvas_fill_ellipse` and `canvas_fill_polygon` work in whole numbers, not
+  double (the S3 does double in software). The ellipse is exact: a pixel is in
+  when `dx2^2 * h^2 <= w^2 * (h^2 - dy2^2)` with distances doubled, and a float
+  `sqrt` only starts the search for each row (it is wrong by one at 220 by 21,
+  264 by 23, 312 by 25 and 318 by 181, which the tests pin). The polygon steps
+  each edge's crossing with a quotient and remainder, no division per row, and
+  a pixel on a left edge is in and one on a right edge is out. The old double
+  fill was not consistent at exact ties (a 45 degree edge through integer
+  vertices): it left stray hatch marks on Qix's thin sliver polygons, so Qix
+  and Pedal re-pinned. Sizes or coordinates past 32768 and 2^24 keep the
+  double code. Neither is measured on the device yet.
 - A colour pixmap is a `Canvas`, and every drawing primitive draws on the
   drawable it is given (`xshim_target` in `pixmap.c`); `None` draws nothing,
   and a bitmap takes only `XCopyArea`, `XCopyPlane` and filled rectangles and

"""Ranks the hacks in a serial log of one rotation lap by where their time goes.

Flash a build with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=20`, log the serial port for the whole lap
(about 20 seconds a hack), then:

    uv run tools/triage_hacks.py lap.log
    uv run tools/triage_hacks.py lap.log --soft    # add soft-double call counts

A frame is `step` (the hack), `push` (the display) and `wait` (what is left of
the delay the hack asked for after the push is credited). Each hack is put in
the first class that fits:

- paced: `wait` is longer than `step`, so the hack asked for its rate. A faster
  step changes nothing unless the delay is also changed (Forest, Vines).
- push-bound: `push` is longer than `step`. Only fewer rows or a smaller push
  help.
- step-bound: `step` is the biggest part. These are the ones to look into.

`--soft` reads the device build's objects (`pio run -e stopwatch` first) for
the soft-double calls in the hack's own object, so a step-bound hack with a
count is a wrapper candidate. A hack the table calls step-bound with no calls
is in its drawing, not its maths.
"""

import argparse
import re
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

RUN = re.compile(r"^run (?P<hack>\S+) (?P<fields>.*)$")
FIELD = re.compile(r"(\w+)=([-\d.]+)")


@dataclass
class Row:
    hack: str
    windows: int
    fps: float
    worst_fps: float
    step: float
    push: float
    wait: float
    kind: str


def parse(text: str) -> dict[str, list[dict[str, float]]]:
    """The `run` windows for each hack, in order."""
    out: dict[str, list[dict[str, float]]] = defaultdict(list)
    for raw in text.splitlines():
        if m := RUN.match(raw.strip()):
            fields = {k: float(v) for k, v in FIELD.findall(m.group("fields"))}
            out[m.group("hack")].append(fields)
    return out


def classify(step: float, push: float, wait: float) -> str:
    if wait > step:
        return "paced"
    if push > step:
        return "push-bound"
    return "step-bound"


def summarise(runs: dict[str, list[dict[str, float]]], skip: int = 1) -> list[Row]:
    """One row a hack. The first window holds the boot and the name overlay, so
    it is left out when the hack has more than one."""
    rows = []
    for hack, windows in runs.items():
        kept = windows[skip:] or windows

        def mean(key: str) -> float:
            return sum(w.get(key, 0.0) for w in kept) / len(kept)

        step, push, wait = mean("step"), mean("push"), mean("wait")
        rows.append(
            Row(
                hack,
                len(kept),
                mean("fps"),
                min(w.get("fps", 0.0) for w in kept),
                step,
                push,
                wait,
                classify(step, push, wait),
            )
        )
    return rows


def soft_counts() -> dict[str, int]:
    """Soft-double calls per object stem, from the device build."""
    sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent))
    import softdouble_report as sd

    counts: dict[str, int] = {}
    for obj in sd.BUILD.rglob("*.o"):
        if "hacks/" not in str(obj):
            continue
        found = sd.soft_calls(obj)
        counts[obj.name.split(".")[0]] = sum(sum(c.values()) for c in found.values())
    return counts


def soft_for(hack: str, counts: dict[str, int]) -> int:
    """The calls in objects whose name starts with the hack's, in any wrapper."""
    key = hack.lower()
    return sum(n for stem, n in counts.items() if stem.startswith(key))


def render(rows: list[Row], counts: dict[str, int] | None) -> str:
    order = {"step-bound": 0, "push-bound": 1, "paced": 2}
    rows = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (order[r.kind], -r.step))
    head = "| Hack | Class | fps | worst | step | push | wait |"
    rule = "| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |"
    if counts is not None:
        head += " soft |"
        rule += " --- |"
    lines = [head, rule]
    for r in rows:
        line = (
            f"| {r.hack} | {r.kind} | {r.fps:.1f} | {r.worst_fps:.1f} | "
            f"{r.step:.1f} ms | {r.push:.1f} ms | {r.wait:.1f} ms |"
        )
        if counts is not None:
            line += f" {soft_for(r.hack, counts)} |"
        lines.append(line)
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n")[0])
    ap.add_argument("log", type=Path)
    ap.add_argument("--soft", action="store_true", help="add soft-double counts")
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)
    rows = summarise(parse(args.log.read_text(errors="replace")))
    sys.stdout.write(render(rows, soft_counts() if args.soft else None))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

    assert rows["Gears"].step == 50.0

    assert th.soft_for("Vines", counts) == 2

import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))

import triage_hacks as th

LOG = """\
boot noise
run Vines fps=2.0 step=180.0ms push=3.0ms sync=0.0ms wait=190.0ms rows=80
run Vines fps=2.6 step=182.0ms push=1.0ms sync=0.0ms wait=180.0ms rows=80
run Vines fps=2.8 step=184.0ms push=1.0ms sync=0.0ms wait=178.0ms rows=80
run Gears fps=5.0 step=30.0ms push=40.0ms sync=0.0ms wait=0.0ms rows=466
run Gears fps=6.0 step=40.0ms push=30.0ms sync=0.0ms wait=0.0ms rows=466
run Gears fps=8.0 step=60.0ms push=30.0ms sync=0.0ms wait=0.0ms rows=466
run Pyro fps=30.0 step=1.0ms push=31.0ms sync=0.0ms wait=0.0ms rows=466
"""


def test_it_collects_windows_per_hack_and_ignores_other_lines():
    runs = th.parse(LOG)
    assert sorted(runs) == ["Gears", "Pyro", "Vines"]
    assert [w["fps"] for w in runs["Vines"]] == [2.0, 2.6, 2.8]


def test_a_longer_wait_than_step_is_paced():
    assert th.classify(step=10, push=3, wait=11) == "paced"


def test_a_longer_push_than_step_is_push_bound():
    assert th.classify(step=10, push=31, wait=0) == "push-bound"


def test_otherwise_the_step_is_the_bottleneck():
    assert th.classify(step=50, push=31, wait=0) == "step-bound"


def test_equal_step_and_wait_is_not_paced():
    assert th.classify(step=10, push=3, wait=10) == "step-bound"


def test_a_push_longer_than_the_wait_is_not_paced():
    assert th.classify(step=10, push=31, wait=20) == "push-bound"


def test_the_first_window_is_left_out():
    rows = {r.hack: r for r in th.summarise(th.parse(LOG))}
    assert rows["Vines"].fps == 2.7
    assert rows["Vines"].worst_fps == 2.6
    assert rows["Gears"].step == 50.0


def test_a_hack_with_one_window_keeps_it():
    rows = {r.hack: r for r in th.summarise(th.parse(LOG))}
    assert rows["Pyro"].fps == 30.0


def test_step_bound_hacks_come_first_slowest_step_first():
    out = th.render(th.summarise(th.parse(LOG)), None).splitlines()
    names = [line.split("|")[1].strip() for line in out[2:]]
    assert names == ["Vines", "Gears", "Pyro"]


def test_soft_counts_add_every_object_that_starts_with_the_hack_name():
    counts = {"xspirograph_single": 4, "xspirograph": 40, "vines_single": 2}
    assert th.soft_for("XSpirograph", counts) == 44
    assert th.soft_for("Vines", counts) == 2

"""Ranks the hacks in a serial log of one rotation lap by where their time goes.

Flash a build with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=20`, log the serial port for the whole lap
(about 20 seconds a hack), then:

    uv run tools/triage_hacks.py lap.log
    uv run tools/triage_hacks.py lap.log --soft    # add soft-double call counts

A frame is `step` (the hack), `push` (the display) and `wait` (what is left of
the delay the hack asked for after the push is credited). Each hack is put in
the first class that fits:

- paced: `wait` is the biggest part, so the hack asked for its rate. A faster
  step helps by exactly what it saves, but the frame cannot get under the
  delay (Forest 500 ms, Vines 200 ms).
- push-bound: `push` is the biggest part. Only fewer rows or a smaller push
  help.
- step-bound: `step` is the biggest part. These are the ones to look into.

`--soft` reads the device build's objects (`pio run -e stopwatch` first) for
the soft-double calls in the hack's own object, so a step-bound hack with a
count is a wrapper candidate. A hack the table calls step-bound with no calls
is in its drawing, not its maths.
"""

import argparse
import re
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

RUN = re.compile(r"^run (?P<hack>\S+) (?P<fields>.*)$")
FIELD = re.compile(r"(\w+)=([-\d.]+)")


@dataclass
class Row:
    hack: str
    windows: int
    fps: float
    worst_fps: float
    step: float
    push: float
    wait: float
    kind: str


def parse(text: str) -> dict[str, list[dict[str, float]]]:
    """The `run` windows for each hack, in order."""
    out: dict[str, list[dict[str, float]]] = defaultdict(list)
    for raw in text.splitlines():
        if m := RUN.match(raw.strip()):
            fields = {k: float(v) for k, v in FIELD.findall(m.group("fields"))}
            out[m.group("hack")].append(fields)
    return out


def classify(step: float, push: float, wait: float) -> str:
    if wait > step and wait > push:
        return "paced"
    if push > step:
        return "push-bound"
    return "step-bound"


def summarise(runs: dict[str, list[dict[str, float]]], skip: int = 1) -> list[Row]:
    """One row a hack. The first window holds the boot and the name overlay, so
    it is left out when the hack has more than one."""
    rows = []
    for hack, windows in runs.items():
        kept = windows[skip:] or windows

        def mean(key: str) -> float:
            return sum(w.get(key, 0.0) for w in kept) / len(kept)

        step, push, wait = mean("step"), mean("push"), mean("wait")
        rows.append(
            Row(
                hack,
                len(kept),
                mean("fps"),
                min(w.get("fps", 0.0) for w in kept),
                step,
                push,
                wait,
                classify(step, push, wait),
            )
        )
    return rows


def soft_counts() -> dict[str, int]:
    """Soft-double calls per object stem, from the device build."""
    sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent))
    import softdouble_report as sd

    counts: dict[str, int] = {}
    for obj in sd.BUILD.rglob("*.o"):
        if "hacks/" not in str(obj):
            continue
        found = sd.soft_calls(obj)
        counts[obj.name.split(".")[0]] = sum(sum(c.values()) for c in found.values())
    return counts


def soft_for(hack: str, counts: dict[str, int]) -> int:
    """The calls in objects whose name starts with the hack's, in any wrapper."""
    key = hack.lower()
    return sum(n for stem, n in counts.items() if stem.startswith(key))


def render(rows: list[Row], counts: dict[str, int] | None) -> str:
    order = {"step-bound": 0, "push-bound": 1, "paced": 2}
    rows = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (order[r.kind], -r.step))
    head = "| Hack | Class | fps | worst | step | push | wait |"
    rule = "| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |"
    if counts is not None:
        head += " soft |"
        rule += " --- |"
    lines = [head, rule]
    for r in rows:
        line = (
            f"| {r.hack} | {r.kind} | {r.fps:.1f} | {r.worst_fps:.1f} | "
            f"{r.step:.1f} ms | {r.push:.1f} ms | {r.wait:.1f} ms |"
        )
        if counts is not None:
            line += f" {soft_for(r.hack, counts)} |"
        lines.append(line)
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"


def main(argv: list[str]) -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n")[0])
    ap.add_argument("log", type=Path)
    ap.add_argument("--soft", action="store_true", help="add soft-double counts")
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)
    rows = summarise(parse(args.log.read_text(errors="replace")))
    sys.stdout.write(render(rows, soft_counts() if args.soft else None))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

input.old_string:
calling `canvas_fill_ellipse`, whose `double` maths is software on the S3. A
  test pins the pixels to `canvas_fill_ellipse`.
input.new_string:
calling `canvas_fill_ellipse` (which used to do `double` maths per row, in
  software on the S3; see below). A test pins the pixels to
  `canvas_fill_ellipse`.
- `canvas_fill_ellipse` and `canvas_fill_polygon` work in whole numbers, not
  double (the S3 does double in software). The ellipse is exact: a pixel is in
  when `dx2^2 * h^2 <= w^2 * (h^2 - dy2^2)` with distances doubled, and a float
  `sqrt` only starts the search for each row (it is wrong by one at 220 by 21,
  264 by 23, 312 by 25 and 318 by 181, which the tests pin). The polygon steps
  each edge's crossing with a quotient and remainder, no division per row, and
  a pixel on a left edge is in and one on a right edge is out. The old double
  fill was not consistent at exact ties (a 45 degree edge through integer
  vertices): it left stray hatch marks on Qix's thin sliver polygons, so Qix
  (612 pixels) and Pedal (3) re-pinned. Sizes or coordinates past 32768 and
  2^24 keep the double code. On the board (step, before to after): Bouboule
  14.5 to 5.2 ms (27.4 to 36.8 fps), Qix 14.6 to 1.9 ms (37.3 to 70.1 fps),
  Pedal 21.8 to 8.6 ms (it then holds the picture for 5 s).
- Lisa is the counter-example to "the stroker maths is the cost" (#98).
  `stroke.c`'s hot path was already float, and converting a slanted segment's
  ends from int straight to float moved Lisa by nothing (52.1 ms before and
  after). With the line calls compiled out its step is 5.2 ms, so 47 ms of 52
  is drawing: 1,396 segments, 6.7k spans and 16k pixels a frame at width 2 and
  13k spans and 65k pixels at width 8. About 3.6 us a span against about 0.1
  us a pixel in a sequential full-frame write suggests each scattered span pays
  a PSRAM cache-line miss (a cost per line touched, not per pixel). Not
  proved: the way to test it is the PSRAM and data-cache settings (speed, line
  size, cache size), which no hack can change.

input.new_string:
wrapper's object for `__muldf3` and friends with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm`.
  `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` does that for every object in
  the device build, by function: a count in a per-frame function is a literal
  or a macro the header could not reach. It lists none in Galaxy, Discrete,
  Drift, Flame, Substrate or Interaggregate now.
- Four things hide soft double from `single_precision.h`, each found by that
  report. `frand` (`single_frand.h`) and `MAXRAND`, `M_PI`, `M_PI_2` and
  `M_PI_4` (`single_constants.h`) are macros with a decimal literal in their
  body, past the literal pass; both headers are opt-in, since each moves the
  wrapper's frames and pins. Exponent literals (`1e-6`, `1.0E5`) were skipped
  by `float_literals.py` until Drift and Flame showed one each. A struct
  declared with `double` fields before the rename keeps them, so a float
  `corners[j].x * size` plus a `double` `pos.x` is a software add: HexTrail's
  `XYZ` (from `normals.h`) was 94 calls in `draw_hextrail`. Give the hack its
  own float struct under the same name, and `normals.h` another name for the
  double one (`hextrail_single_gl.c`; frames byte-identical). And a trig
  argument that is a big whole number cannot be a float: XSpirograph's second
  angle is millions of degrees and Vines' is an `int` in the billions, so a
  plain `double` to `float` turned both pictures to noise. XSpirograph reduces
  its angles mod 360 in integers at build time (`tools/xspirograph_patch.py`);
  Vines builds `(double) a` as `(long) a`, so its `cos` macro gets the exact
  integer and takes the phase as a 64-bit multiply by 2^64 / 2 pi, wrapping
  into whole turns (`vines_single.c`). Look at a frame before trusting a
  float build of anything whose angles grow. To find the line of a stray
  promotion, add `-Wdouble-promotion -fsyntax-only` to a file's compile
  command in `firmware/compile_commands.json` (`pio run -e stopwatch -t
  compiledb`; delete the file afterwards, it upsets the editor).

`0.81` stay double too, and a header cannot change them: `0.5 * x` with a
  float `x` is software double maths. Check the wrapper's object for soft-double
  helpers with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm braid.o | grep ' U __.*df'` (compile with
  `-Os -mlongcalls` and the shim's include paths). If any remain, rewrite the
  literals at build time as Braid does: `tools/float_literals.py` (tested, skips
  strings and comments) run by `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, and the
  wrapper includes `<name>_floatlit.c` from the build directory. GCC's
  `-fsingle-precision-constant` does the same, but Apple clang ignores it, so
  host tests would run other arithmetic than the board.
- Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame and Substrate were wrapped before this check
  and have not been looked at for double literals.
- Hand-written `sin` and `cos` (`hacks/fast_trig.h`) moved Braid by 5%. Do the
  literals first.
- Compare double and float frames at several counts. Early frames match; a
  chaotic hack diverges later but should keep its look.
- GL hacks too: Hypnowheel's spiral called `cos` and `sin` in `double` for
  every vertex, about 275 ms of a 706 ms step, hidden behind a fill-heavy look.
  Its wrapper (`hypnowheel_single_gl.c`) adapts `get_position` and
  `get_rotation` as HexTrail's does.
- Results: Galaxy 5 to 14 fps. Substrate step 119-121 ms to 37-38 ms, 6.2 to
  12.5 fps.

# Porting an xscreensaver hack

The rules live in `AGENTS.md` ("Rules", "Gotchas") and the path-scoped notes in
`.claude/rules/`. This skill sets the order of work and the points to stop. The
numbered steps are in `adding-a-hack.md` and the recipes it names are in
`techniques.md`, both next to this file. For several hacks in one go, read
`batches.md` too.

## 1. Pick, then read the source

Take S-rated rows from `docs/porting-assessment.md` first, and prefer a low
**Speed** band: the table runs each unported S hack on the host. The effort
rating counts missing shim calls, not memory, speed or stack (Braid was S, and
would have shown as high). A high band is a hack that will probably run slowly
on the board; a low band is not a guarantee, because a hack still doing
software `double` maths runs far slower on the device than on the host. Read
the hack's source before copying it, and look for:

| The source has | Technique (seen in) |
| --- | --- |
| Arrays or a state over a few MB | Build-time patch (Maze) |
| `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `double` in a hot loop | Single precision (Galaxy, Substrate) |
| Locals over a few KB | Stack check (Rorschach) |
| An allocation of 100 KB or more, or `exit()` on failure | Large allocations (Substrate) |
| Pixmaps, clip masks, a logo image | Images (Maze) |
| A hack that restarts itself | Restart leak test (Maze, Substrate) |
| A `free` that relies on state `draw` sets up (a lazy `initted`) | Stopping before the first draw (Blaster) |
| Hairlines, fades or `glPolygonOffset` in a GL hack | Thin lines in a GL hack |
| Xft text (`XftDrawStringUtf8`) | Xft text (XJack) |
| Threads, shared memory | Skipping a hack |
| A licence header | Read it; add a notices section only if it differs from jwz's |

## 2. Set up

Work in a worktree off `origin/main`. Its setup and the commands it refuses are
in "Worktree setup".

## 3. Red, copy, green

Follow `adding-a-hack.md`. Show the registry test failing before
copying. Fill each shim gap test-first, then break the code on purpose and
watch the test fail ("Tests that cannot be fooled"). Filling a missing
function is a shim gap. Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a
shared helper) is not: stop and ask Rod first. A speed-up in the shared GL
layer counts too, even when every pinned frame hash still matches (HexTrail's
deferred depth clear): ask before writing it, and name it in the PR body.

## 4. Verify on the host

Run `pio test -e native`, `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`
and `uv run tools/check_notices.py`, and dump frames at several counts. Host
frames cannot show a byte swap, which happens in the push to the display: judge
colour on the device, on a colour you know the answer to.

## 5. Device

Flash only after Rod says so in this conversation; approval for one flash is
not approval for the next. See "Device capture". Report "compiles", "host tests
pass" and "runs on the device" separately; only Rod can say what the screen
shows. If it is slow, measure, change one thing, flash again and compare; if it
is still slow, say so and suggest dropping it. A hack that runs at a good rate
can still go: Rod dropped Boing (8.3 fps, "pretty boring on a small screen")
and asked for HexTrail to be tuned because it fell under 10 fps before the
rotation moved on. Judge a hack on a 466 px round screen, and by its worst
window as well as its mean. Record the numbers in
`tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, marking anything unmeasured as such.

## 6. Deliver

Commit named paths. Open the draft PR with `entire trail create` and put what
is unverified in its body. After a rebase, a push needs `--force-with-lease`:
ask Rod each time. Rod approves and merges; then delete the branch and
fast-forward `main`. New gotchas go in the matching `.claude/rules/` file (or
`AGENTS.md` if they apply everywhere) in the same PR, and deferred
ideas become issues.

## Red flags

| Thought | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| "It is rated S, so I need not read it" | Maze was rated L for Xlib gaps; the real blocker was a 20 MB `calloc`. |
| "It compiles, so it works" | Rorschach compiled and rebooted on its first frame. |
| "The colours look right" | Not from a host frame: every hack was byte swapped until Maze. |
| "My test passes, so it tests something" | A test through Pyro passed with the runner broken. Break the code on purpose. |
| "AGENTS.md says to fix shim gaps, so I can change the runner" | A new function is a gap. A change every hack sees needs Rod. |
| "Rod approved flashing earlier" | Ask again for each flash. |
| "Single precision is done, so the hack is as fast as it gets" | HexTrail gained 0.3 fps from it and 2.3 from a depth clear in the GL layer. Read what the shared code does each frame. |
| "The mean is above 10 fps" | HexTrail's mean was 15.3 and its worst window 10.8; its step grew all cycle. Read the lowest window. |

content.text:
Both branches are committed and tested. Nothing is pushed, there is no PR, and I haven't flashed a normal rotating build yet.

**Board state:** the last flash was the Lisa A/B, and its second variant had the line drawing compiled out. It's probably showing a blank, pinned Lisa, so say if you want me to flash a normal rotating build.

## Branches

| Branch | Native tests |
| --- | --- |
| `feature/shim-integer-fills` (ellipse, polygon, stroker, docs) | 797 of 797 |
| `feature/hack-wrappers` (wrappers, tools, docs) | 792 of 792, plus 595 Python tests |

They merge cleanly. `feature/soft-double-investigation` is still there as the record, and I can delete it whenever you like.

## Results on the board

All numbers are step time (before to after), with the fps change where it moved.

**Shim branch**
- **Bouboule:** 14.5 to 5.2 ms (27.4 to 36.8 fps), from the integer ellipse.
- **Qix:** 14.6 to 1.9 ms (37.3 to 70.1 fps), from the integer polygon.
- **Pedal:** 21.8 to 8.6 ms. It then holds each picture for 5 s, so its fps barely moves.
- **Lisa:** no change (52.1 ms before and after). With the line calls compiled out its step is 5.2 ms, so 47 of 52 ms is drawing. The cost is about 3.6 µs per span against about 0.1 µs per pixel in a sequential write.

**Wrapper branch**
- **Vines:** 182 to 10.3 ms (2.6 to 5.0 fps), which is now its own 200 ms delay.
- **XSpirograph:** 44 to 10.9 ms (12.0 to 16.9 fps). That mean includes the hack's own 5 s and 1 s holds.
- **Hopalong:** 7-20 to 3.4 ms (19-25 to 68 fps).
- **WhirlWindWarp:** 6-26 to 3.8 ms (17-25 to 56 fps).
- **BinaryHorizon:** 95.8 to 31.8 ms (8.3 to 17.1 fps).
- **Barcode:** 77 to 56 ms (9.6 to 13.1 fps), with identical frames.
- **Anemone:** 30.5 fps on the survey lap, against 11-15.5 before.

I also tried Bouboule as a single-precision wrapper and dropped it. Its step stayed at 14.5 ms, because the cost was the ellipse fills.

**Float traps:** XSpirograph and Vines turned to noise when I first built them in float. Their trig arguments are huge whole numbers, which a float can't hold.
- XSpirograph's angles are now reduced mod 360 in integers at build time.
- Vines reduces its integer to a phase in 64-bit fixed point.
- I looked at frames before pinning either.

## The waits you asked about

The runner credits only the push against a hack's requested delay, so a frame is the step plus the delay. That makes some slow hacks paced by design rather than slow: Forest's 500 ms and Vines's 200 ms. A faster step still shortens the frame, but never below the delay. Changing a delay changes how the hack looks, so that's your call.

## Process proposals

1. **Done:** `tools/triage_hacks.py` takes a 20-second-per-hack rotation lap and sorts each hack into step-bound, push-bound or paced, with its soft-double call count. It has tests, and I mutation-checked it. The port-hack skill and `hacks.md` now say to run the soft-double report on every wrapper and a triage lap after every batch.
2. **The lap showed where not to look:** the biggest steps (Braid 170 ms, Marbling 158, BinaryRing 93, Discrete 92) have zero soft-double calls, so they're bound by their drawing, not by doubles.
3. **Proposal:** scattered PSRAM writes look expensive, and that would also explain Discrete. I'd test the PSRAM speed and data-cache settings (cache size and line size) as a separate experiment. It touches the board config for every hack, so I haven't started it.
4. **Not done:** `score_hacks.py` could flag hacks that still use `double`, and the Speed column could say when a hack is paced by its own delay. Say if you want either.

## Left alone

- **Deluxe `draw_star`:** left for last, as agreed.
- **Kumppa:** it's memory-bound (row copies in PSRAM).
- **Interference:** its inner loop is integer table work, with no soft calls in it.
- **GL hacks (Gears, Morph3D, UnknownPleasures, GraphStat):** their maths is small beside the rasteriser.

## Decisions for you

- Push both branches and open draft PRs? I'd keep them as two PRs.
- Do you want Deluxe `draw_star` next, or the PSRAM cache experiment first?

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/worktrees/soft-double-investigation/.claude/skills/deliver-branch

# Delivering a branch

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `entire trail create --title ... --type feature --body ...` pushes the branch
  (`--type` takes only `bug`, `feature` or `task`; `chore` is refused)
  and opens a linked DRAFT PR. The PR body is not synced from the trail: update
  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body, then read the PR back (`gh pr view N --json body`):
  #27 merged with the generic body, so `Fixes #23` never reached GitHub and
  the issue stayed open until it was closed by hand.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`. Confirm the merge
  after a fresh `git fetch`: a stale `origin/main` says "not merged". Remove
  the branch's worktree first (a checked-out branch cannot be deleted), and
  note that `git branch -d` refuses while local `main` is behind, so check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main` and then use `-D`. `main` is
  usually checked out in Rod's main checkout, so `git fetch origin main:main`
  is refused there: run `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in it, only if
  `git status` shows no tracked changes.
- Merge with `gh pr ready N` then `gh pr merge N --merge` once Rod approves
  (trail PRs are drafts). His approval is enough: do not wait for the Entire
  Gates check to finish. A stacked PR's gate
  can fail "Up to date: 1 commit behind" once its parent merges: if approvals
  and findings pass and the PR is mergeable, merge it, with no rebase.
- Before merging, `git fetch` and compare the PR's `headRefOid` with your tip:
  Rod sometimes pushes to the branch (docs commits, a merge of `main`). Read
  what arrived with `git log --oneline <tip>..origin/<branch>`, and clean up
  from the merge commit, not your last push. After `ExitWorktree keep` the
  tool names the branch `worktree-<name>`; the real branch is
  `git worktree list`'s.
- A review of fixed code can raise a new finding on the fix itself (a clamp
  that did not stop a wrap). Reproduce it with a failing test before changing
  the code, and mutation-check each branch of the new guard.
- `entire agent-help` says trails are unavailable; `entire trail create` works.
  Write a PR body to a file for `gh pr edit --body-file` (an apostrophe in an
  inline `--body '...'` must be `'"'"'`).
- `gh pr edit N --body-file` replaces the whole body, including the
  `<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->` ... `-end -->` block at the top. Keep that
  block in the file, or the PR loses its trail.
- Findings: `entire trail finding list N`, then `... resolve N <id> -m "..."`.
  Bot reviews can lag about 20 minutes. `N` is the trail number (PR #12 was
  trail 6), not the PR number. For a false positive or upstream behaviour in a
  byte-identical hack, use `entire trail finding dismiss N <id> -m "<reason>"`.
- To file your own review's findings: `entire trail finding add --trail N
  --client-id <key> --severity high|medium|low --file <path> --start-line A
  --end-line B -m "<body>"` (no title flag; the client id makes a re-run safe).
  Open the body by saying an agent filed it for Rod.
- In a worktree session create the trail with a one-line `--body`, then set the
  real body with `gh pr edit N --body-file` (keep the trail-link block), and
  check `closingIssuesReferences` with `gh pr view N --json` (it can lag a
  few seconds).
- `entire trail update --body` takes no number and acts on the current
  branch (`entire trail update 8` errors).
- Stacked PR: `entire trail create --base <parent-branch>`. When the parent
  merges, `gh pr edit N --base main` before deleting its branch, then
  `git rebase --onto origin/main <old parent tip>`. The rebased push needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod first), unless the branch was never pushed.
- `docs/porting-assessment.md` conflicts on rebase: `git checkout --theirs`
  it to continue, then rerun `tools/score_hacks.py` and amend the result in.
- Two ports in flight both append to `g_hacks[]`, so whichever merges second
  conflicts in `registry.c`, the expected list in `test_hacks.c`,
  `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, `tools/assessment_measured.md.in` (rows,
  paragraphs and the hack count) and the three `build_src_filter` lines in `platformio.ini`,
  as well as the generated assessment. Keep both sides, put the newer hack
  last, and regenerate the assessment. A rebased published branch needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod), and GitHub can reject that push once too.
- A finding that says the code "does not exist" can be stale after a rebase
  (the skill PR was reviewed before the Blaster and Substrate code it referred
  to had landed). Check it against `main` before dismissing, and put the
  evidence in the dismissal. Entire's approvals gate once showed "no reviewers
  have approved" right after a force push, though Rod had approved; his word is
  enough, so say so and go ahead.
- `entire trail finding list` can show one open "Review verdict ... approve"
  finding: it is the reviewers' verdict, not a defect. `mergeStateStatus`
  reads UNSTABLE while the gate runs, and Rod's approval is enough.
- A shared-code PR (stroker, runner, canvas) can move pins of hacks merged
  since it branched: merge or rebase onto `main` and rerun the pin loop before
  judging frames (Celtic joined #89's moved set after #88 landed).
- Why a gate is red: `gh api
  repos/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/commits/<branch>/check-runs
  --jq '.check_runs[]|.output.summary'`.
  "Approvals: failed" is just Rod not having approved yet, and "Checks:
  skipped" is normal (no CI here). `entire trail watch` streams forever, so to
  watch poll `gh pr view N`, that API and `entire trail finding list N` from a
  script file under a Monitor, printing only on change. Merge only when Rod
  says to, even once the gates are green.
- If `entire trail create` reports "failed to push branch", run
  `git push -u origin <branch>` and rerun it: the trail is then created.
- Run `gh pr ready N` and `gh pr merge N --merge` as separate commands: on a
  PR that is already ready, `ready` exits non-zero and skips a chained merge.
  Confirm with `gh pr view N --json state`.

Written by Claude, an agent working under Rod's direction.

Fixes #75. Fixes #59. Refs #54.

The hack-wrapper half of the soft-double sweep. The shared-shim half (integer
ellipse and polygon fills, for #57 and #74) is its own branch and PR, so the
two can land or be dropped separately; they merge cleanly together.

## What changed

- **Missed soft double.** `single_precision.h` renames `double`, but not
  `frand`, `MAXRAND`, `M_PI` and friends (macros with a decimal literal in the
  body), exponent literals such as `1e-6`, or structs declared `double` before
  the rename. New opt-in `single_constants.h`; `float_literals.py` now floats
  exponent literals; HexTrail gets a float `XYZ`.
  Interaggregate, Galaxy, Discrete, Drift, Flame, Substrate and HexTrail now
  show no soft-double calls in per-frame functions.
- **New single-precision wrappers:** XSpirograph, Vines, Hopalong,
  WhirlWindWarp, BinaryHorizon (added to the existing 24-bit wrapper) and
  Barcode. Two of them needed more than a rename: their trig arguments are
  whole numbers in the millions or billions, which a float cannot hold.
  XSpirograph reduces its angles mod 360 in integers at build time
  (`tools/xspirograph_patch.py`); Vines builds `(double) a` as `(long) a` and
  takes the phase with a 64-bit multiply.
- **Anemone** erased the whole window every frame (217k of its 229k pixels
  written). It now erases only where last frame's lines were, with identical
  frames.
- **Tools:** `tools/softdouble_report.py` (soft-double calls per function from
  the device objects) and `tools/triage_hacks.py` (sorts a 20 s-a-hack rotation
  lap into step-bound, push-bound and paced, with soft-double counts). Rules
  and the port-hack skill say when to run them.
- Bouboule was tried and dropped: its step stayed at 14.5 ms (ellipse fills).

## Measured on the board

Step before to after (mean of 5-6 windows, pinned build, rotation off).

| Hack | Step | fps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vines | 182 to 10.3 ms | 2.6 to 5.0 (its own 200 ms delay) |
| XSpirograph | 44.2 to 10.9 ms | 12.0 to 16.9 (includes its 5 s and 1 s holds) |
| Hopalong | 7.3-20.1 to 3.4 ms | 19-25 to 68 |
| WhirlWindWarp | 6.2-26.4 to 3.8 ms | 17-25 to 56 |
| BinaryHorizon | 95.8 to 31.8 ms | 8.3 to 17.1 |
| Barcode | 77.1 to 56.1 ms | 9.6 to 13.1 |
| Anemone | 31-56 to 25.2 ms | 11-15.5 to 30.5 (worst window 20.4) |

Anemone is from one 20 s window on a rotation lap, not a pinned run. The
Galaxy, Discrete, Drift, Flame, Substrate, Interaggregate and HexTrail changes
were checked for soft-double calls and frame identity on the host, but not
A/B-timed against main on the board.

## Frames

- Byte-identical to the double build at the frame counts checked: Anemone,
  HexTrail, Barcode, Hopalong, Interaggregate-style literal fixes where
  noted in their commits.
- Rounding moves a few pixels: XSpirograph (about 50 at frame 50), Vines,
  BinaryHorizon (112 and 348 bytes of 434 KB), WhirlWindWarp (later frames,
  where its random stars land). I looked at each; pins re-taken for
  XSpirograph, Vines and BinaryHorizon.

## Verification

- `pio test -e native`: 792 of 792. `pytest tools/tests`: 595 passed, 1
  skipped. Device build compiles.
- New tests are mutation-checked (the triage tool's seven mutants all killed,
  after two tests were added for survivors).

## Not done

- Deluxe `draw_star` (#54 idea 5): still double, left for its own change.
- Hacks whose cost is drawing or memory, not maths (Braid, Marbling, Discrete,
  BinaryRing, Kumppa, Interference) are untouched.
- Forest (500 ms) and Vines (200 ms) are paced by their own delays; changing
  those changes how they look, so it is Rod's call.

Written by Claude, an agent working under Rod's direction.

Fixes #57. Fixes #74. Refs #98.

The shared-shim half of the soft-double sweep: `canvas_fill_ellipse` and
`canvas_fill_polygon` now work in whole numbers, because the ESP32-S3 does
`double` in software. It changes what every hack that fills an ellipse or a
polygon sees, so it is separate from the hack-wrapper PR (they merge cleanly
together).

## What changed

- **`canvas_fill_ellipse`** is exact and integer. A pixel is inside when
  `dx2^2 * h^2 <= w^2 * (h^2 - dy2^2)` with distances doubled. A float `sqrt`
  only gives the starting guess per row, and two exact loops correct it (it is
  off by one at 220 by 21, 264 by 23, 312 by 25 and 318 by 181; the tests pin
  those). Pixel-identical to the old fill, so no pinned frame moved. Sizes over
  32768 keep the double path.
- **`canvas_fill_polygon`** steps each edge's crossing with a quotient and
  remainder, with no division per row. A pixel on a left edge is in and one on
  a right edge is out. Coordinates beyond 2^24 keep the double path.
- **The old polygon fill was not consistent at exact ties** (a 45 degree edge
  through integer vertices). It left stray hatch marks on Qix's thin sliver
  polygons. The new fill removes them, so **Qix (612 pixels) and Pedal (3)
  re-pinned**, after looking at the frames before and after.
- **`stroke.c` `slanted()`** converts a segment's ends straight from `int` to
  `float`, not through `double`.

## Measured on the board

Step before to after (mean of 4-6 windows, pinned build, rotation off).

| Hack | Step | fps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bouboule (ellipse) | 14.5 to 5.2 ms | 27.4 to 36.8 |
| Qix (polygon) | 14.6 to 1.9 ms | 37.3 to 70.1 |
| Pedal (polygon) | 21.8 to 8.6 ms | 9.8 to 10.1 (it holds each picture for 5 s) |
| Lisa (stroker) | 52.1 to 52.1 ms | 14.3 to 14.3 |

The "before" figures are from the same board earlier the same day, on `main`.

## #98 (Lisa and the stroker)

The premise did not hold: `stroke.c`'s hot path was already float, and the
conversion above moved nothing. With the line calls compiled out Lisa's step is
5.2 ms, so 47 of its 52 ms is drawing: 1,396 segments a frame, 6.7k spans and
16k pixels at width 2, 13k spans and 65k pixels at width 8. About 3.6 us a
span against about 0.1 us a pixel in a sequential write suggests each scattered
span pays a PSRAM cache-line miss. That is not proved; the PSRAM and data-cache
settings are the next experiment. #98 stays open.

## Verification

- `pio test -e native`: 797 of 797 under AddressSanitizer.
- New tests: the ellipse against the double reference for every size to 48 at
  three offsets, 4000 random sizes to 3000 against an exact check, six sizes
  where the float estimate is off, big and clipped sizes; the polygon against
  an exact integer reference on random polygons up to 1000 vertices plus 45
  degree, triangle and "thirds" slopes. Mutation-checked: two mutants survive,
  both equivalent (an upward-loop `<=` versus `<` that no size to 900 reaches,
  and a polygon carry `>=` versus `>`).
- Device build compiles. Only the four hacks above were timed on the board;
  other users of the shared fills (anything calling `XFillArc` or
  `XFillPolygon`) have host frames checked by the pins but no timing.

have zero soft-double calls; their cost is drawing/PSRAM, not maths.

table loop), GL hacks (rasteriser dominates). Forest (500 ms) and Vines
(200 ms) are paced by their own delays; changing those is Rod's call.

content.text:
Trails 61 and 62 are merged (PRs #109 and #110), and the PSRAM experiment is still running.

**Merge**
- #109 (wrappers) and #110 (shim) were both ready, and each head matched my tip.
- Both tips are in `origin/main`, which is now at 147b898.
- The remote and local `feature/hack-wrappers` and `feature/shim-integer-fills` branches are deleted.
- #57, #59, #74 and #75 are closed. #98 stays open, deliberately.
- I haven't fast-forwarded your main checkout: I work from the worktree, so that's yours to do.
- `feature/soft-double-investigation` is still there as the record. Its commits were cherry-picked, so git can't tell they've landed. Say if you want it deleted.

**PSRAM experiment**
- `experiment/psram-cache` is uncommitted and branched from the shim tip before the merge. I'll rebase it when it's worth keeping.
- **Cost model:** every data-cache miss costs about 0.92 µs, whatever the write size. That works out at about 35 MB/s sequential, and the 32 KB cache size shows clearly in the working-set test.
- **64-byte lines (benchmark):** sequential writes and reads are about 28% faster. Spans under 16 pixels are 20-45% slower.
- **Prefetch:** the ROM prefetch setting I tried did nothing.
- **Lisa on the board:** step is unchanged with 64-byte lines (52.1 vs 52.3 ms), and its push is 13% faster (13.4 vs 11.6 ms).
- **Running now:** 64-byte lines against the default on 14 hacks (Discrete, Qix, Anemone, Interference, Kumppa, Braid, Marbling, BinaryRing, Gears, Pyro, Morph3D, Galaxy, Deluxe, HexTrail). It takes about 40 minutes and I'll report the table when it finishes.
- I'll try a few more prefetch settings afterwards, since my first guess may simply have been a bad one.

I also updated my project memory to reflect the merge.

| Marbling | 5.4 → 5.8 | 157.7 → 148.9 ms | 28.9 → 24.6 ms |
| Braid | 6.8 → 6.9 | 141.7 → 142.0 ms | 20.1 → 17.4 ms |
| Gears | 15.0 → 15.5 | 55.6 → 53.9 ms | 9.3 → 8.1 ms |
| BinaryRing | 10.8 → 11.1 | 70.8 → 73.2 ms | 27.1 → 23.2 ms |
| Qix | 69.7 → 71.6 | 1.88 → 2.00 ms | 10.5 → 9.8 ms |
| Galaxy | 12.7 → 12.9 | 57.5 → 56.3 ms | 14.6 → 13.2 ms |
| Morph3D | 14.7 → 14.7 | 57.4 → 57.1 ms | 3.8 → 3.4 ms |
| Discrete | 7.4 → 7.0 | 117.5 → 124.4 ms | 11.3 → 10.0 ms |
| Pyro | 83.8 → 82.5 | 0.68 → 0.85 ms | 1.12 → 1.25 ms |

**Pushes:** a full-frame push drops from about 29 ms to 24.8 ms. That's the single biggest effect, and it applies to every hack that pushes much of the screen. Pushes read the canvas sequentially, which is where the longer line helps.

**Steps:** hacks that fill or copy areas speed up by 3-12% (Interference, Deluxe, Marbling, Kumppa). Scatter-heavy ones get slightly worse: Discrete's step is 6% slower and Pyro's 0.2 ms slower. That matches the benchmark, where short isolated writes pay more per miss.

**Net:** every hack except Discrete and Pyro gains fps (Discrete loses 5%, Pyro 1.7%).

**Caveats**
- One round of about 35 seconds per hack, so differences under about 3% are noise.
- The setting is a ROM call the SDK says not to make from an application. I only call it at the start of `setup()`, and none of the hacks crashed.
- I haven't checked it against the TE-synced push (Unknown Pleasures), where the push timing was tuned to the old line size. That needs its own check.

I'll add the HexTrail row when it lands.

**Decision for you:** if you want this adopted, I'd put it behind a build flag (on by default) in its own PR, with the Unknown Pleasures check and a longer multi-round run on the two losers and a few winners first. The alternative is to leave it as an experiment while I try the other prefetch settings.

octal PSRAM, 32 KB 8-way D-cache), sequential write about 35 MB/s. 64-byte
